overview: This file consists of an American consular report by Stuart E. Grummon describing prison administration in the Kwantung Leased Territory after a visit to the prison at Dairen. It surveys the prison population by nationality and offense, the Russian- and Japanese-era buildings, industrial labor, food and medical care, discipline, recreation, accommodation, and punishments—including whipping—and comments on political prisoners and six European inmates, five of whom faced death sentences for piracy and murder. Although Grummon concludes that the institution was clean, orderly, and outwardly well administered, his closing observation implies that its effective discipline rested partly on coercion rather than persuasion.

subfiles.title: Report on Prison Administration in the Kwantung Leased Territory
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul, Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Grummon reports on the population, physical conditions, labor, discipline, punishments, and administration of the prison at Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Following a prison visit, Grummon records approximately 770 inmates—about half Japanese, 30 percent Chinese, and 20 percent Korean—and notes both ordinary crimes and imprisonment for unorthodox political ideas. He describes clean Russian- and Japanese-era facilities, extensive industrial labor, adequate food and medical care, strict silence, limited recreation, road work in shackles, and punishments ranging from reduced rations to solitary confinement and whipping. He also reports six European prisoners, including four Germans and a Swiss condemned to death for piracy and murder. His generally favorable assessment of the prison's outward administration ends with a guarded suggestion that its discipline was not maintained entirely through persuasive means.

interest: Shows a Kwantung colonial prison's mix of disciplined order, forced labor, and harsh punishment, including foreign capital cases.
